problem: Tic-tac-toe variants : Given the width of a tic-tac-toe board, what is the smallest dimension such that X is guaranteed to have a winning strategy?
missing_details: Precise definition of the d-dimensional hypercube board of side length n (the set of cells indexed by d-tuples from {1,…,n})
Definition of a combinatorial line (an affine line of n cells obtained by fixing all but one coordinate) as the winning pattern
Specification that two players X and O alternate placing markers on empty cells, with X moving first under optimal play
Clarification that the game is a draw if all cells are filled without either player completing a line
refined_question: Let n≥1 be a given integer. Consider the following two-player game played on the set of cells {(i₁,…,i_d): i_j∈{1,…,n} for j=1,…,d}. Players X and O alternate turns placing their symbol on an unoccupied cell, with X playing first. A combinatorial line is any collection of n cells whose coordinates are of the form (a₁,…,a_{k−1},t,a_{k+1},…,a_d) as t ranges over {1,…,n}, for some fixed index k and fixed values a_j for j≠k. A player wins immediately upon occupying all n cells of some line; if the board becomes full without any player having won, the game ends in a draw. For each n, define d(n) to be the minimum dimension d for which X has a forced win under optimal play. Determine d(n) for each n (or establish bounds on d(n)).
justification: The canonical statement of the open problem appears verbatim in the Wikipedia article “n^d game” under the heading “Game theory” as an unsolved problem in mathematics. The refined question expands this to a precise, self-contained description by introducing the parameters n and d, defining the game board, the notion of a combinatorial line as the winning condition, the rules of alternating play with X starting, and the draw condition. No equivalent formulation is given in the source.
